html:
On 14 October 1956 at Nagpur, B. R. Ambedkar became a Buddhist, and in the following days he converted several hundred thousand Dalits, the people once called untouchables, in a mass ceremony. It began the Dalit Buddhist movement.

Ambedkar had fought caste all his life, from the Mahad Satyagraha of 1927 to drafting the Constitution of India. In 1935 he said he would not die a Hindu. After twenty years of study he chose Buddhism, the faith of Ashoka, which had almost vanished from India, as a religion with no caste in it.

He gave the converts 22 vows that rejected Hindu gods and rituals. His version, later called Navayana, read the Buddha's teaching as social and political. Ambedkar died seven weeks later, but the movement grew, and most of India's Buddhists today, many of them in Maharashtra, trace their faith to that day.
